newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq says sanctions may cause "horrendous disaster".
newsitem.headline: Iraq says sanctions may cause "horrendous disaster".

text.p: Iraq has told the United Nations that economic sanctions threaten its society with a "horrendous disaster that may lead to its collapse" and accused the United States of attempting genocide.
This was because the Iraqi people were "deprived of such means of survival of food and medicine and other basic necessities and because the supply situation has reached subsistence levels."

In a 14-page memorandum to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali published on Wednesday, Iraq gave statistics detailing what it said were the effects of sanctions on living conditions, health and educational standards.

The sanctions, which bar the export of Iraqi oil and the import of most goods except food, medicine and other strictly humanitarian items, were imposed shortly after Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"The suffering of the Iraqi people has reached a point where it can no longer be ignored or overlooked because it now threatens to bring upon the society as a whole a horrendous disaster that may lead to its collapse," the memorandum said.

A prime condition for lifting the curbs is a clean bill of health from a U.N. special commission in charge of scrapping Iraq's nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic weapons potential. The commission is still not satisfied Iraq has provided full details of its clandestine weapons programmes.
"Iraq holds the United States fully responsible for the sufferings of the Iraqi people through its insistence on maintaining the economic embargo," the Iraqi paper said.

"There is no room for doubt that the United States is intentionally endeavouring to annihilate the Iraqi people," it added, saying the "civilized world has determined that genocide, whether committed in time of peace or war, is a crime under international law that must be prevented and punished."

Iraq also accused the United States of trying to prevent the implementation of a plan, agreed with the United Nations in May, to enable Baghdad to export $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, to buy badly needed civilian goods.

The plan had been expected to be in effect by now. But Boutros-Ghali said on Sept. the security situation in northern Iraq, where Iraqi troops were involved in inter-Kurdish fighting, prevented the deployment of U.N. staff to monitor the scheme.
Iraq said even this partial easing of sanctions would not "in reality meet the minimum needs of the population."

Alluding to U.S. retaliation for the dispatch of Iraqi troops into the Kurdish-inhabited region for the first time since the end of the Gulf War, Iraq said the U.S. "attempt to undermine the ... oil-for-food formula by launching its treacherous missile attack on Iraq on September 3 and 4 1996 will inevitably lead to increased suffering for the Iraqi people."

Iraq called on United States to "halt its constant aggression against Iraq, desist from interfering in Iraq's internal affairs, and strive for the implementation" of the oil-for-food plan as quickly as possible as a first step towards the total lifting of the economic embargo.
It said the sanctions were no longer justified since Iraq has discharged its obligations under the relevant Security Council resolutions.
